rationale: B wins because it is tighter and less drunk on its own cleverness. A has useful material, but it keeps turning holes into angles, especially "The AI upgrade boutique fitness startups promised just shipped from the incumbent instead" without naming a single challenger or proof that anyone promised it. B's "Mindbody's new AI cut studio no-show rates 22% by texting the waitlist" is a cleaner trade story with the right proof burden attached, even if the headline should say the company claims it happened in a pilot.
gaps_in_A: "Mindbody's AI treats 50,000 studios' booking calendars as one data set" overstates the facts. The update says Mindbody has booking data and 50,000 studios/salons, not that it pools them into one data set.
"vertical-software private-equity ownership" invents ownership color from "privately held after a take-private deal." Maybe true, maybe not. You do not pitch maybe.

"The AI upgrade boutique fitness startups promised" is an unsupported competitor narrative. The set even admits it needs "at least one named standalone AI-scheduling competitor," which means the angle is not ready.
"it's adding AI to both" is too strong. The facts do not say the assistant touches ClassPass.
gaps_in_B: "cut studio no-show rates 22%" should be softened to "Mindbody says" and "in a pilot." Otherwise it launders vendor-reported data into fact.
"AI sits on top of both" makes the same ClassPass leap A makes. The facts say Mindbody owns ClassPass, not that the assistant runs on or affects it.
"using aggregated booking data across the network" is not supplied. The update says booking data; it does not say network-wide aggregation.
The next step says `journalist-fit-check`, but the actual blocker is proof: pilot methodology, one named studio, and the ClassPass boundary. Fit-checking reporters before that is premature.
